- Replicates Benzon's core experiment design
    - Same single-word prompt "story" used to elicit outputs
    - Same single-session vs. separate-session comparison, 10 stories each
    - Reuses Benzon's own paper as ground truth to check whether findings generalize to open-source LLMs
- Tests Benzon's central claims empirically with new models
    - Claim 1 (single session → more name variety, e.g. "Elara") is checked with Llama-3.1-8B and found broadly supported
    - Claim 2 (prototypical story = abstraction over training corpus) is tested by comparing Llama/DeepSeek outputs
        - DeepSeek's very different default story (no fairy-tale prototype, no named protagonists) is used as direct evidence for Benzon's claim that the prototype reflects training data, not a universal narrative default
    - Claim 3 (studying outputs matters as much as studying internals) is adopted as the sidenote's own methodological stance
        - Explicitly reuses Benzon's blackbox / "olive-pitter" analogy from the paper to justify the behavioral (input-output) approach over mechanistic interpretability
- Extends Benzon's qualitative observations into a quantitative rubric
    - Turns Benzon's implicit story elements (exploration, return, community benefit) into an explicit 8-criterion scoring table (Home, Departure, Magical World, Helpers, Challenge, Growth, Return, Community Benefit)
    - Adds a "coherence" dimension Benzon's paper doesn't address, showing smaller/weaker models degenerate under the bare "story" prompt
- Adds new variables Benzon didn't test
    - Prompt phrasing ("story" vs. "tell me a story" vs. "write a story")
    - Model scale/family comparison (Llama-3.1-8B vs. Llama-3.3-70B vs. DeepSeek-V4-Flash)
- Draws an explicit throughline to Benzon's earlier working paper ("reverse engineering" version)
    - Connects that paper's five-part story structure (Donné, Disturb, Plan/Transit, Enact, Celebrate) to this paper's prototype elements (Home, Departure, Journey/Quest, magical world, return, community benefit)
    - Notes both papers share the same underlying question: what is ChatGPT's default story and how consistent/coherent is it
- Frames Benzon's approach within a broader methodological family
    - Links Benzon's blackbox treatment of ChatGPT to Ramesh/Dori's blackbox/glassbox/whitebox framework for characterizing vision-system performance, casting Benzon's prototypical-story method as one instance of empirical, output-based system characterization
